canonicalExplanation.summary: **Specificity** is a score in three columns, compared **left to right**: (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements). `#nav` is (1,0,0); `.card .title` is (0,2,0); `h2` is (0,0,1). It's not one total number — one ID beats any number of classes. When specificity ties, the **later** rule wins. Keep selectors low and flat so components are easy to override without `!important`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Your card titles should be navy, but they stay black. A teammate's global `h2 { color: black; }` is winning? No — your `.card-title` class should beat it. Unless… Let's learn to compute the score. A component class beats a type selector without needing an id or !important escalation. In this lesson you'll explain and repair a specificity conflict without adding unnecessary !important declarations.

```predict
{"question": "Which wins: `#main p` or `.article .content .text p`?", "options": ["The four-part class selector (it has more parts)", "#main p — one ID beats any number of classes"], "answer": 1, "why": "(1,0,1) vs (0,3,1). The first column is compared first, and 1 > 0. Columns never carry over."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Elements, attributes and nesting** and **Origins, importance and layers** — specificity is only compared when origin, importance and layer are tied.

sections.heading: The rule: compare columns left to right
sections.body:
| Selector | (IDs, classes, types) |
|---|---|
| `h2`. | (0,0,1). |
| `.card-title`. | (0,1,0). |
| `.card h2`. | (0,1,1). |
| `nav a:hover`. | (0,1,2). |
| `#nav a`. | (1,0,1). |
| `:where(.card) h2`. | (0,0,1) — :where adds nothing. |

Inline `style=""` beats all selectors; `!important` jumps to a higher tier altogether.

```reveal
{"prompt": "Do 11 classes beat 1 ID?", "answer": "No. (0,11,0) vs (1,0,0): the ID column is compared first. Specificity isn't a single number where 10 classes = 1 ID."}
```

sections.heading: Repair without escalation

includes: Calculate specificity as (IDs, classes, types) and compare left to right.
Fix conflicts with classes, order or layers instead of IDs and !important.

outcomes: Explain and repair a specificity conflict without adding unnecessary important declarations.

examples.title: A class beats a type selector
examples.situation: A component class beats a type selector without needing an id or !important escalation.
walkthrough: **Conflict:** global `h2 { color: black; }` (0,0,1) vs component `.card-title { color: navy; }` (0,1,0).
**Compare:** the class column 1 beats 0, so `.card-title` wins regardless of order.
**Why it looked wrong:** the HTML used `class="card_title"` — a typo meant the selector didn't match. Fix the class name; the browser will render navy.
examples.result: The component class wins by specificity, with no ID or !important escalation needed.

examples.title: The !important arms race
examples.situation: A site has `.btn { background: blue !important; }`. A new `.btn-danger { background: red; }` never applies, so a developer adds `!important` there too — then another rule needs it as well.
walkthrough: The first !important moved .btn above every normal declaration.
Each fix adds another !important, making overrides ever harder.
Repair: remove !important, keep .btn and .btn-danger at equal specificity, and put the variant after the base.
examples.result: The danger button turns red through normal source order, and no !important remains.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Specificity is one total number where ten classes always equal one ID.
misconceptions.correction: Specificity is compared column by column: IDs first, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then types. Any number of classes loses to a single ID; columns never carry over.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why did the one-ID selector win?

analogy.example: Specificity is like **comparing version numbers**: 1.0.1 beats 0.11.0 because the first number is checked first, no matter how big the second one is.
usefulFor: seeing why classes never add up to an ID
limitations: Versions change over time; specificity is fixed by the selector.
Ties go to the later rule, like a newer release date.

steps.explanation: The global type selector has one type.
The component class has one class.
A component class beats a type selector without needing an id or !important escalation.

expectedEvidence: No unnecessary !important or ID overrides remain.

remediation.explanation: In DevTools, hover a selector to see its specificity. Write both scores side by side and compare column by column. If they tie, check which comes later.

recap.summary: To explain and repair a specificity conflict, score selectors as (IDs, classes, types), compare left to right, and let source order break ties. Fix conflicts with matching classes, order or layers rather than unnecessary !important declarations.
